newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Focus of Korea scandal shifts to president's son.
newsitem.headline: Focus of Korea scandal shifts to president's son.

text.p: South Korea's political storm has gathered new strength as the focus of a loans-for-kickbacks scandal that has rocked the nation now shifts to the son of beleaguered President Kim Young-sam.

State prosecutors, reopening a probe into the scandal involving failed Hanbo Steel Co, said on Saturday they would delve into rumours that Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, took a 200 billion won ($226 million) kickback.
"South Korea is turning a dangerous corner," said Shin Jung-hyun, political science professor at Kyunghee University.
"The next three to four months will be a critical period. It is virtually impossible to forecast tomorrow in national politics," he said.

The announcement adds to the growing sense of crisis caused by parliament's launch on Friday of a 45-day inquiry into the scandal, labour unions plans to fight for wage increases in April and May, and simmering campus unrest as students prepare for traditional spring anti-government protests.

The collapses of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co last week, together with weeks of labour strikes in January, have stoked fears of further bankruptcies and dashed hopes for an economic revival.
Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik said the nation should brace for economic growth of only about five percent this year, against rises of 7.1 percent last year and 8.9 percent in 1995.
Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, is at the heart of the parliamentary inquiry into the collapse of Hanbo Steel under debts totalling $5.8 billion.

The opposition has charged that top officials pressured banks into providing loans to Hanbo Steel despite insufficient collateral and the company's poor prospects, and that the officials received kickbacks from Hanbo in return.
The bankruptcy was South Korea's biggest corporate casualty.

Opposition parties said the parliamentary inquiry would also cover the collapse of Sammi Steel under similar circumstances. They have raised suspicions of influence peddling by Hyun-chul in the Sammi case as well.
A prosecution official said Park Tae-jung, a businessman suspected of managing money for the president's son, was to be questioned by prosecutors in the Hanbo case.

Police on Friday raided Park's home and offices to confiscate boxes of papers and computer discs to investigate charges by the opposition that Park, acting as an agent for Hanbo, funnelled money to the president's son in return for help in securing loans.
Lawmaker Lim Chae-jung of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics accused Hyun-chul of raising a slush fund of up to one trillion won through such influence peddling.
The government on Friday appointed senior prosecutor Shim Je-ryoon to head the new probe into Hanbo.
He replaces Choi Byung-koog, who led an earlier investigation resulting in indictments of 10 people, including a former cabinet minister and close aides to president Kim.
But Choi's probe exonerated the president's son, a move slammed by the opposition as a whitewash of the case aimed at covering up complicity at the highest levels.
"I'll show the prosecution's determination to carry out a transparent and fair investigation," Shim told reporters.

Shim would not give details on the new investigation but state television said each suspicious aspect of Hanbo's collapse would be revisited. Officials of five major creditor banks of the company are due to be summoned for questioning this week, prosecutors said.
"President Kim appears to have realised that further cover-ups could bring about unfortunate consequences for him," said Moon Chung-in, who lectures on politics at Yonsei University.

Kim, who is barred by the constitution from seeking a second term in presidential elections in December, put former presidents Chun Doo-hwan and Roh Tae-woo on trial for corruption and human rights abuses. Chun has been jailed for life and Roh for 17 years.
(Conversion: $1 = 883 won)
